title: Validation and Policy Enforcement
readerIntent: Understand how Nodics prevents invalid or unauthorized changes across every entry path.
owner: Each capability owns its rules; Nodics validation, security, and pipeline layers enforce shared contracts
summary: Validation protects data shape and business invariants, while policy enforcement decides whether an authenticated principal may perform an operation in the resolved context.

sections.heading: What is Validation and Policy Enforcement?
paragraphs: Validation checks whether input, state, relationships, and requested changes satisfy the rules owned by a capability. It prevents malformed, unauthorized, inconsistent, or unsafe data from becoming accepted business state.
Think of an application form reviewed at several checkpoints: basic format, business eligibility, ownership, and cross-record rules are distinct checks and may produce different recovery guidance.

sections.heading: Business value
items: Apply the same rule to APIs, imports, jobs, workflows, BackOffice, and internal services.
Reject invalid data before it corrupts authoritative records or derived indexes.
Separate human login from service-to-service and scheduled-process authentication.
Explain failures with stable codes while protecting sensitive details.
Allow customer projects to add stricter rules through governed extension points.

sections.heading: Validation is not authorization
paragraphs: Validation asks whether the request and intended state are structurally and logically valid. Authentication establishes an identity. Authorization and access policy determine whether that identity may act on the target. A successful result in one layer never bypasses the others.

sections.heading: Validation responsibilities
items: Transport validation checks request shape, headers, parameters, and representation.
Schema validation checks types, required values, formats, defaults, and declarative constraints.
Relationship validation checks that references exist and may be associated in the resolved scope.
Business validation protects lifecycle transitions and domain invariants.
Provider and runtime-governance validation protect infrastructure and activation contracts.

sections.heading: Policy responsibilities
items: Authentication establishes a human, service, or scheduled principal.
Authorization decides whether the principal may perform the operation.
Tenant and ownership policy limits the available records and context.
Field and operation permissions restrict what can be read or changed.
Approval and audit policy controls sensitive changes beyond CRUD permission.

sections.heading: One rule, one authority
paragraphs: A rule lives at the lowest authoritative boundary reached by every relevant mutation. A required string belongs in schema metadata; an allowed state transition belongs in the owning business service or interceptor; permission belongs in authorization.
Frontend validation improves usability but cannot replace backend enforcement. Import, job, event, workflow, API, and BackOffice paths converge on the same rules.

sections.heading: Example: activating an employee
paragraphs: Transport checks the employee identifier. Schema validation ensures active is Boolean. Business validation rejects activation when mandatory profile data is incomplete. Authorization restricts activation to approved employee groups in the correct tenant.
Axis may disable the button or show guidance, but the Profile mutation enforces every rule for every caller.

sections.heading: Safe failure and evidence
items: Return a stable registered status without leaking secrets or protected records.
Preserve authorized trace and diagnostic context and avoid partial state.
Test valid, missing, malformed, duplicate, and boundary values.
Test unauthorized, wrong-tenant, wrong-owner, and forbidden-field access.
Test invalid transitions and consistency across API, import, event, job, workflow, and BackOffice paths.
